messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Arjun

Arjun was twenty when his older cousin Rohan died. It was a Tuesday in March, unremarkable except for the phone call from his mother, her voice fractured in a way he had never heard before. Rohan had been driving home from work—a software engineer, stable, careful, the kind of person everyone said had his life figured out. A drunk driver crossed the median on the interstate. Rohan was pronounced dead at the scene. There had been no warning, no illness, no time to say anything. One moment he existed; the next, he didn't. For Arjun, who had grown up in the same house as Rohan during his childhood, who had watched him navigate college and career with a steadiness Arjun secretly envied, the event shattered something fundamental about how he understood safety. The world, he had come to believe, was a place where ordinary Tuesday mornings could end in death. Randomness was the only rule.

In the weeks after the funeral, Arjun tried to write. He had been working on a novel—a small literary project he had been quietly proud of—but the words felt hollow now, contaminated by the knowledge that none of it mattered if everything could be taken away without reason. He abandoned the manuscript. More pressingly, when his parents began asking him about college applications, about whether he would apply for jobs, about what came next, Arjun found himself unable to answer. The future felt like a trap. If he made plans, if he allowed himself to imagine anything—a career, a relationship, a life—he was only setting himself up for devastation. So he stopped planning. He refused to discuss it. His mother would ask if he had looked at internships; he would change the subject or leave the room. The avoidance felt necessary, protective. Not planning meant nothing could be taken from him.

Yet the avoidance created its own torment. Without plans, without forward motion, Arjun felt unmoored, and that formlessness fed a deepening conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that he was powerless within it. His inability to imagine a future began to feel like evidence that no future was worth imagining—that nothing he did mattered, that safety was an illusion. He became hypervigilant in ways he did not fully recognize. Sounds made him jump: a car horn outside his window would send adrenaline flooding through his chest. He could not relax even when sitting alone in his bedroom with the door locked. His body seemed to expect catastrophe at every moment. Sleep became nearly impossible. He would lie awake for hours, his mind cycling through scenarios—car crashes, sudden illnesses, the random violence that had taken Rohan. When he did sleep, he woke gasping.

The avoidance of grief reminders became another layer of the trap. Anything connected to Rohan—a song that had played at the funeral, the software company's logo glimpsed in an advertisement, even the sight of someone driving a silver sedan like Rohan's—triggered a wave of panic and despair. So Arjun began to avoid more and more. He stopped going to the coffee shop where he used to write because Rohan had taken him there once. He declined invitations to family gatherings where relatives might mention Rohan's name. He isolated himself, telling himself this was the only way to manage the grief, but what actually happened was that his world grew smaller and his conviction that he was fundamentally unsafe grew larger.

By late summer, five months after Rohan's death, Arjun was stuck in a cycle he could not name. The more he avoided—the future, reminders, social situations—the more his belief that the world was dangerous and that he was helpless intensified. And the more convinced he became of that danger, the more he needed to avoid, to seek reassurance from his parents that he was okay, that nothing bad would happen to him. He would call his mother at work and ask her to confirm he was safe, and for a few minutes after she reassured him, the panic would subside. But it always returned, sharper each time. His parents, alarmed by his deterioration, finally insisted he see someone. Arjun came to the first appointment exhausted and terrified, unable to articulate why he felt so broken, only knowing that he had lost not just his cousin but his ability to believe in tomorrow.

violation_explanations: Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: While the vignette describes negative appraisals (the world is dangerous, randomness is the only rule, the future is a trap, safety is an illusion) and maladaptive strategies (avoidance of planning, avoidance of reminders, isolation), no paragraph explicitly conveys that the appraisals drive or lead to the avoidance behaviors. The causal direction is unclear or implicit rather than explicitly stated.

Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: Although maladaptive strategies (avoidance) and threat perception (hypervigilance, panic, sense of danger) both appear, the vignette does not clearly establish that the avoidance behaviors themselves intensify the sense of threat. The cycle is described ("the more he avoided... the more his belief that the world was dangerous... intensified"), but this relationship is stated only in the final paragraph in a general summary form and lacks explicit causal language connecting the avoidance to increased threat perception within a coherent explanatory frame.
